# PRECEPTOR — M2 calculator fixtures, plausibility ranges and rule tables

*Generated by `scripts/fixtures-doc.ts` from the calculator definitions and a run of their tests (each case below is marked with its result in that run). Do not edit by hand.*

This is the list offered for review by a qualified pharmacist (M2 plan, Section 8). Every test value has a recorded origin, given in the test title:

- **published** — a worked example in a named published source;
- **hand** — the arithmetic is written out in the title or the test;
- **independent** — computed by `scripts/calc-crosscheck.py`, a separate Python implementation written from the cited formula (not from the TypeScript code);
- tests without a number check behaviour: refusals, unit handling, warnings, boundaries.

Validation manifest: generated 2026-10-19T21:08:52.024Z; engine tests passed 64, failed 0. A calculator is shown in the app only with a passing record for its exact formula version and an unchanged engine.

Plausibility ranges are deliberately wide: they catch unit slips and typing errors and are not reference ranges. A value outside one is used only after the trainee confirms it, with the value and unit shown. A value outside the definitional limits is rejected.

## Calculators

### Creatinine clearance (Cockcroft–Gault) — `crcl_cg@1`

- Formula: CrCl (mL/min) = (140 − age) × weight (kg) ÷ (72 × SCr (mg/dL)), × 0.85 if female
- Citation: Cockcroft DW, Gault MH. Prediction of creatinine clearance from serum creatinine. Nephron 1976;16(1):31–41. Ideal body weight: Devine BJ. Gentamicin therapy. Drug Intell Clin Pharm 1974;8:650–655.
- Tests: 11 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: Assumes stable creatinine; unreliable in acute kidney injury and in patients on dialysis. Derived in adult men; the 0.85 factor for women was an assumption of the authors. Low muscle mass (older age, malnutrition, amputation) can make creatinine low and the estimate high. Do not round creatinine up automatically — follow your reference. Not the same as eGFR: do not substitute one for the other in drug dosing.

| Sex | yes | — | — | — |
| Weight (total body weight) | yes | kg | 2 – 300 | 0.2 – 700 |
| Serum creatinine | yes | mg/dL | 0.2 – 20 | 0.01 – 50 |
| Weight used in the formula (choice: Total body weight (TBW) / Ideal body weight (IBW, Devine) / Adjusted body weight (AdjBW)) | yes | — | — | — |
| Height | optional | cm | 45 – 230 | 1 – 300 |
| Adjustment factor for adjusted body weight — asked when weightBasis is adjbw | optional | unitless | 0.2 – 0.5 | 0.01 – 1 |

### eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021, creatinine) — `egfr_ckdepi2021@1`

- Formula: eGFR = 142 × min(SCr/κ, 1)^α × max(SCr/κ, 1)^−1.200 × 0.9938^age × 1.012 (if female); κ = 0.7 (female) or 0.9 (male); α = −0.241 (female) or −0.302 (male); SCr in mg/dL
- Citation: Inker LA, Eneanya ND, Coresh J, et al. New creatinine- and cystatin C–based equations to estimate GFR without race. N Engl J Med 2021;385(19):1737–1749.
- Tests: 10 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: Assumes stable creatinine; not valid in acute kidney injury or on dialysis. Less accurate at extremes of muscle mass (amputation, cachexia, very high muscle mass). Adults only (18 years or older).

| Serum creatinine | yes | mg/dL | 0.2 – 20 | 0.01 – 50 |

### Ideal and adjusted body weight (Devine) — `ibw_adjbw@1`

- Formula: IBW = 50 kg (male) or 45.5 kg (female) + 2.3 kg × (height in inches − 60); AdjBW = IBW + factor × (TBW − IBW)
- Citation: Devine BJ. Gentamicin therapy. Drug Intell Clin Pharm 1974;8:650–655. Adjusted body weight = IBW + factor × (TBW − IBW), with the factor of the reference in use.
- Tests: 8 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: Which weight a drug is dosed on, and which adjustment factor, comes from the drug’s reference — not from this calculator. Not for children: the Devine formula is for adults.

### Vancomycin AUC₂₄ (two levels, Sawchuk–Zaske) — `vancomycin_auc@1`

- Formula: ke = ln(C1/C2) ÷ (t2 − t1); Cmax = C1·e^(ke·(t1 − end of infusion)); Cmin = C2·e^(−ke·(next dose − t2)); V = (Dose/tinf)·(1 − e^(−ke·tinf)) ÷ (ke·(Cmax − Cmin·e^(−ke·tinf))); CL = ke·V; AUC₂₄ = (Dose × 24/τ) ÷ CL
- Citation: Sawchuk RJ, Zaske DE. Pharmacokinetics of dosing regimens which utilize multiple intravenous infusions: gentamicin in burn patients. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm 1976;4(2):183–195. Targets and warnings: Rybak MJ, Le J, Lodise TP, et al. Therapeutic monitoring of vancomycin for serious methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infections: a revised consensus guideline and review by the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists, the Infectious Diseases Society of America, the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society, and the Society of Infectious Diseases Pharmacists. Am J Health Syst Pharm 2020;77(11):835–864.
- Tests: 24 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1) · high-risk calculation: extended tests and an escalation message
- Limitations shown with every result: Needs two levels in the same dosing interval, both after the end of the infusion, with exact draw times and the exact start of the infusion. Not for patients on dialysis or CRRT, and not before steady state. Where levels cannot be measured, use the separate calculator "Vancomycin without levels" (the department’s method).

| Start of that infusion (day and clock time) | yes | — | — | — |

### Vancomycin without levels (empiric dose and interval) — `vancomycin_empiric@2`

- Formula: Dose (mg) = dose per kg (15–20 mg/kg) × actual body weight (kg). Interval, by the department’s table (CrCl by Cockcroft–Gault, as a whole number): above 90 mL/min every 8 h; 50–90 every 12 h; 20–49 every 24 h; below 20, or on dialysis, one dose, then dosing by levels. Daily dose (mg/24 h) = dose × 24 ÷ interval (h)
- Citation: Method and table set by the department: owner decision 6 (18 October 2026) — empiric weight-based dosing, 15–20 mg/kg of actual body weight per dose, the interval from Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance — and the department’s interval table (owner decision, 19 October 2026). Creatinine clearance: Cockcroft DW, Gault MH. Prediction of creatinine clearance from serum creatinine. Nephron 1976;16(1):31–41. Ideal body weight: Devine BJ. Gentamicin therapy. Drug Intell Clin Pharm 1974;8:650–655.
- Tests: 14 passed, 0 failed (formula version 2) · high-risk calculation: extended tests and an escalation message
- Limitations shown with every result: The interval is the department’s table (owner decision, 19 October 2026), for adults: above 90 mL/min every 8 h; 50–90 every 12 h; 20–49 every 24 h; below 20 mL/min, or on dialysis, one dose, then dosing by levels. A population-based starting regimen for a setting where levels cannot be measured, not a patient-specific one. When levels can be measured, use the AUC calculator. No loading dose and no maximum single dose are applied: follow your hospital’s protocol. Unreliable when creatinine is changing (acute kidney injury): Cockcroft–Gault assumes a stable creatinine. Adults only.

### Phenytoin corrected for albumin (Sheiner–Tozer) — `phenytoin_corrected@1`

- Formula: Corrected level = measured level ÷ (0.2 × albumin (g/dL) + 0.1); in severe renal failure: measured level ÷ (0.1 × albumin (g/dL) + 0.1)
- Citation: Sheiner LB, Tozer TN. Clinical pharmacokinetics: the use of plasma concentrations of drugs. In: Melmon KL, Morrelli HF, eds. Clinical Pharmacology: Basic Principles in Therapeutics. 2nd ed. New York: Macmillan; 1978. Renal-failure form: Liponi DF, Winter ME, Tozer TN. Renal function and therapeutic concentrations of phenytoin. Neurology 1984;34(3):395–397.
- Tests: 14 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1) · high-risk calculation: extended tests and an escalation message
- Limitations shown with every result: An estimate. A measured free (unbound) phenytoin level is more reliable whenever it is available. Not valid when another drug displaces phenytoin from albumin (for example valproate): measure a free level. Revised coefficients (for example 0.25 or 0.275 instead of 0.2) and other renal cut-offs have been published; this calculator uses the original equations and the department’s renal definition.

### Child–Pugh score — `child_pugh@1`

- Formula: Points 1/2/3 — bilirubin < 2, 2–3, > 3 mg/dL; albumin > 3.5, 2.8–3.5, < 2.8 g/dL; INR < 1.7, 1.7–2.3, > 2.3; ascites none, slight, moderate–severe; encephalopathy none, grade 1–2, grade 3–4. Class A 5–6, B 7–9, C 10–15.
- Citation: Pugh RNH, Murray-Lyon IM, Dawson JL, Pietroni MC, Williams R. Transection of the oesophagus for bleeding oesophageal varices. Br J Surg 1973;60(8):646–649. INR thresholds replace the original prothrombin-time prolongation, as in common current use.
- Tests: 10 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: Developed to predict surgical risk in cirrhosis, not drug clearance; it does not measure the liver’s capacity to metabolise a given drug. Ascites and encephalopathy are judged subjectively; albumin and INR are affected by infusions, nutrition and anticoagulants. In cholestatic liver disease (for example primary biliary cholangitis) different bilirubin thresholds are used; this calculator uses the standard ones.

| Ascites (choice: None / Slight (or controlled with diuretics) / Moderate to severe (or refractory)) | yes | — | — | — |
| Hepatic encephalopathy (choice: None / Grade 1–2 (or controlled with treatment) / Grade 3–4 (or refractory)) | yes | — | — | — |

### QTc (Bazett) — `qtc_bazett@1`

- Formula: QTc = QT ÷ √RR, with RR = 60 ÷ heart rate (s)
- Citation: Bazett HC. An analysis of the time-relations of electrocardiograms. Heart 1920;7:353–370. Choice between them: Vandenberk B, Vandael E, Robyns T, et al. Which QT correction formulae to use for QT monitoring? J Am Heart Assoc 2016;5(6):e003264.
- Tests: 8 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: Assumes a regular rhythm; with atrial fibrillation or a wide QRS (bundle branch block, pacing) these corrections are unreliable — ask your preceptor. Not an ECG interpretation: the values come from the written report.

### Anion gap (with albumin correction) — `anion_gap@1`

- Formula: AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃); albumin-corrected AG = AG + 2.5 × (4.0 − albumin (g/dL))
- Citation: Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃). Albumin correction: Figge J, Jabor A, Kazda A, Fencl V. Anion gap and hypoalbuminemia. Crit Care Med 1998;26(11):1807–1810.

- Limitations shown with every result: The normal range depends on the laboratory’s analyser; interpret against your laboratory’s range. A gap does not identify the cause; the clinical picture does.

### Calcium corrected for albumin — `corrected_calcium@1`

- Formula: Corrected Ca (mg/dL) = Ca (mg/dL) + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin (g/dL))  [equivalent: Ca (mmol/L) + 0.02 × (40 − albumin (g/L))]
- Citation: Payne RB, Little AJ, Williams RB, Milner JR. Interpretation of serum calcium in patients with abnormal serum proteins. Br Med J 1973;4(5893):643–646.
- Tests: 5 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: Agrees poorly with measured ionised calcium, especially in critical illness and kidney disease. Where ionised calcium can be measured, use it. Laboratories that use a different albumin method may use a local correction.

| Input | Required | Unit (canonical) | Plausible range (confirmation outside) | Definitional limits (rejected outside) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Calcium (total) | yes | mg/dL | 4 – 16 | 0.01 – 30 |
| Albumin | yes | g/dL | 1 – 6 | 0.01 – 10 |

Test cases:

1. ✓ 8.0 mg/dL with albumin 2.0 g/dL → 8.0 + 0.8 × 2.0 = 9.6 mg/dL = 2.395 mmol/L (hand, independent)
1. ✓ in SI units: 2.0 mmol/L with albumin 20 g/L → 2.399 mmol/L, within 0.001 of the SI form 2.0 + 0.02 × (40 − 20)
1. ✓ a high albumin lowers the corrected value (10.0 with albumin 4.5 → 9.6)
1. ✓ refuses without albumin, and warns about different samples
1. ✓ uses only the total calcium, never the ionised one

### Absolute neutrophil count (ANC) — `anc@1`

- Formula: ANC (×10⁹/L) = WBC (×10⁹/L) × (neutrophils % + bands %) ÷ 100
- Citation: ANC = WBC × (segmented neutrophils % + band neutrophils %) ÷ 100 (standard haematology definition).
- Tests: 7 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: If the laboratory’s neutrophil percentage already includes band forms, do not enter bands separately. Use the WBC and differential from the same sample.

| Input | Required | Unit (canonical) | Plausible range (confirmation outside) | Definitional limits (rejected outside) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| White blood cells (WBC) | yes | ×10⁹/L | 0.1 – 200 | 0 – 1000 |
| Neutrophils (%) | yes | % | — | 0 – 100 |
| Band neutrophils (%) | optional | % | — | 0 – 100 |

Test cases:

1. ✓ WBC 5.0, neutrophils 60%, bands 5% → 5.0 × 65 ÷ 100 = 3.25 ×10⁹/L = 3250 cells/µL
1. ✓ without a band count: segmented neutrophils only, and says so (1.2 × 30 ÷ 100 = 0.36)
1. ✓ ×10³/µL is the same unit as ×10⁹/L
1. ✓ refuses percentages adding up to more than 100
1. ✓ a percentage above 100 is rejected outright
1. ✓ refuses without the differential, and an unverified band count blocks too
1. ✓ warns when the count and the differential come from different samples

### CURB-65 — `curb65@1`

- Formula: One point each: confusion; urea > 7 mmol/L; respiratory rate ≥ 30/min; systolic BP < 90 mmHg or diastolic BP ≤ 60 mmHg; age ≥ 65 years
- Citation: Lim WS, van der Eerden MM, Laing R, et al. Defining community acquired pneumonia severity on presentation to hospital: an international derivation and validation study. Thorax 2003;58(5):377–382.
- Tests: 7 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: Derived for adults with community-acquired pneumonia, from findings at presentation; not for hospital-acquired pneumonia or severe immunosuppression. A BUN result is converted to urea (÷ 2.801). The US adaptation counts BUN > 19 mg/dL, which differs for BUN between 19 and 19.6 mg/dL. The score supports, and never replaces, clinical judgement of where to treat.

| Input | Required | Unit (canonical) | Plausible range (confirmation outside) | Definitional limits (rejected outside) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| New confusion | yes | — | — | — |
| Urea (or BUN) | yes | mmol/L | 0.5 – 80 | 0.01 – 300 |
| Respiratory rate | yes | breaths/min | 4 – 60 | 0 – 120 |
| Systolic blood pressure | yes | mmHg | 50 – 260 | 1 – 400 |
| Diastolic blood pressure | yes | mmHg | 20 – 160 | 1 – 300 |
| Age | yes | years | 0 – 120 | 0 – 130 |

Test cases:

1. ✓ every threshold just short → 0
1. ✓ every threshold just met → 5
1. ✓ a diastolic pressure of 60 alone earns the blood-pressure point
1. ✓ score 2 is the intermediate group
1. ✓ BUN is converted to urea (÷ 2.801): BUN 20 mg/dL = 7.14 mmol/L → point; BUN 19.5 = 6.96 → no point
1. ✓ urea reported in mg/dL (urea mass) is converted with ÷ 6.006: 43 mg/dL = 7.16 mmol/L → point
1. ✓ refuses without the confusion answer, the urea, or a blood pressure

### qSOFA — `qsofa@1`

- Formula: One point each: respiratory rate ≥ 22/min; altered mentation (GCS < 15); systolic BP ≤ 100 mmHg
- Citation: Seymour CW, Liu VX, Iwashyna TJ, et al. Assessment of clinical criteria for sepsis: for the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). JAMA 2016;315(8):762–774. Singer M, Deutschman CS, Seymour CW, et al. JAMA 2016;315(8):801–810.
- Tests: 5 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: Not a diagnostic criterion for sepsis, and a score below 2 does not rule it out. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 advises against qSOFA alone as a screening tool (Evans L, et al. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143). Adults outside the ICU; not validated in children.

| Input | Required | Unit (canonical) | Plausible range (confirmation outside) | Definitional limits (rejected outside) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Respiratory rate | yes | breaths/min | 4 – 60 | 0 – 120 |
| Altered mentation (GCS below 15) | yes | — | — | — |
| Systolic blood pressure | yes | mmHg | 50 – 260 | 1 – 400 |

Test cases:

1. ✓ RR 22 → 1; SBP 101 and normal mentation → 0
1. ✓ RR 21, altered mentation, SBP 100 → 2, the higher-risk threshold
1. ✓ all three → 3
1. ✓ states that it is not a diagnostic criterion
1. ✓ refuses without the mentation answer

### CHA₂DS₂-VASc — `cha2ds2vasc@1`

- Formula: C heart failure 1; H hypertension 1; A₂ age ≥ 75 2; D diabetes 1; S₂ stroke/TIA/thromboembolism 2; V vascular disease 1; A age 65–74 1; Sc female sex 1
- Citation: Lip GYH, Nieuwlaat R, Pisters R, Lane DA, Crijns HJGM. Refining clinical risk stratification for predicting stroke and thromboembolism in atrial fibrillation using a novel risk factor-based approach: the Euro Heart Survey on atrial fibrillation. Chest 2010;137(2):263–272.
- Tests: 6 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: For atrial fibrillation without moderate–severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve. The 2024 ESC guideline uses CHA₂DS₂-VA, without the sex point (Van Gelder IC, et al. Eur Heart J 2024;45(36):3314–3414). Whether to anticoagulate is a clinical decision made with the guideline, not by the score.

| Input | Required | Unit (canonical) | Plausible range (confirmation outside) | Definitional limits (rejected outside) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Congestive heart failure or left ventricular dysfunction | yes | — | — | — |
| Hypertension | yes | — | — | — |
| Age | yes | years | 0 – 120 | 0 – 130 |
| Diabetes mellitus | yes | — | — | — |
| Prior stroke, TIA or thromboembolism | yes | — | — | — |
| Vascular disease (prior myocardial infarction, peripheral artery disease or aortic plaque) | yes | — | — | — |
| Sex | yes | — | — | — |

Test cases:

1. ✓ male, 64, no risk factor → 0
1. ✓ female, 75, every risk factor → 1+1+2+1+2+1+1 = 9
1. ✓ age points: 64 → 0, 65 → 1, 74 → 1, 75 → 2; female adds 1
1. ✓ stroke counts 2
1. ✓ refuses when any risk factor is unanswered — never assumed absent
1. ✓ notes the 2024 ESC CHA₂DS₂-VA

### HAS-BLED — `has_bled@1`

- Formula: One point each: uncontrolled hypertension; abnormal renal function; abnormal liver function; stroke; bleeding; labile INR; elderly (> 65 years); drugs; alcohol
- Citation: Pisters R, Lane DA, Nieuwlaat R, de Vos CB, Crijns HJGM, Lip GYH. A novel user-friendly score (HAS-BLED) to assess 1-year risk of major bleeding in patients with atrial fibrillation: the Euro Heart Survey. Chest 2010;138(5):1093–1100.
- Tests: 5 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1)
- Limitations shown with every result: A high score calls for attention to the modifiable risk factors and closer review; on its own it is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation.

| Input | Required | Unit (canonical) | Plausible range (confirmation outside) | Definitional limits (rejected outside) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled hypertension (systolic above 160 mmHg) | yes | — | — | — |
| Abnormal renal function (dialysis, transplant, or creatinine ≥ 2.26 mg/dL / 200 µmol/L) | yes | — | — | — |
| Abnormal liver function (cirrhosis, or bilirubin > 2 × upper limit with AST/ALT/ALP > 3 × upper limit) | yes | — | — | — |
| Prior stroke | yes | — | — | — |
| Prior major bleeding or a predisposition to bleeding | yes | — | — | — |
| Labile INR (unstable or high, or time in therapeutic range below 60%) | yes | — | — | — |
| Age | yes | years | 0 – 120 | 0 – 130 |
| Drugs predisposing to bleeding (antiplatelet agents, NSAIDs) | yes | — | — | — |
| Alcohol excess (8 or more drinks a week) | yes | — | — | — |

Test cases:

1. ✓ age 65, nothing else → 0 (elderly is above 65)
1. ✓ age 66 and every item → 9
1. ✓ age 70, drugs and alcohol → 3, the high-risk threshold; 2 is below it
1. ✓ says a high score is not by itself a reason to withhold anticoagulation
1. ✓ refuses when an item is unanswered

### Infusion rate, weight-based (mcg/kg/min → mL/h) — `infusion_rate_weight@1`

- Formula: Rate (mL/h) = dose rate (mcg/kg/min) × weight (kg) × 60 ÷ concentration (mcg/mL)
- Citation: Formula set by the department (owner decision 9, 18 October 2026): dimensional analysis of a continuous infusion.
- Tests: 11 passed, 0 failed (formula version 1) · high-risk calculation: extended tests and an escalation message
- Limitations shown with every result: Checks arithmetic only: the dose rate, the drug, its dilution and concentration come from the order and your hospital’s preparation protocol. Uses the weight recorded in the case; some drugs are dosed on another weight — follow the drug’s reference. Pump programming and the preparation must be independently double-checked before any infusion.

| Input | Required | Unit (canonical) | Plausible range (confirmation outside) | Definitional limits (rejected outside) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prescribed dose rate | yes | mcg/kg/min | 0.01 – 100 | 0.0001 – 1000 |
| Weight (total body weight) | yes | kg | 2 – 300 | 0.2 – 700 |
| Concentration of the prepared solution | yes | mcg/mL | 1 – 100000 | 0.001 – 1000000 |
| Age | optional | years | 0 – 120 | 0 – 130 |

Test cases:

1. ✓ 5 mcg/kg/min, 70 kg, 1600 mcg/mL → 13.125 mL/h (hand: 5 × 70 = 350 mcg/min × 60 = 21 000 mcg/h ÷ 1600)
1. ✓ 0.1 mcg/kg/min, 80 kg, 64 mcg/mL → 7.5 mL/h (hand: 0.1 × 80 = 8 mcg/min × 60 = 480 ÷ 64)
1. ✓ 10 mcg/kg/min, 60 kg, 4000 mcg/mL → 9 mL/h (hand: 10 × 60 = 600 × 60 = 36 000 ÷ 4000)
1. ✓ 0.05 mcg/kg/min, 50 kg, 16 mcg/mL → 9.375 mL/h (hand: 0.05 × 50 = 2.5 × 60 = 150 ÷ 16)
1. ✓ shows the drug delivered per minute and per hour, and every step
1. ✓ concentration in mg/mL and dose rate in mcg/kg/h give the same result (explicit conversions)
1. ✓ refuses without a weight, a dose rate or a concentration, naming each
1. ✓ rejects an unknown unit and an impossible value; an implausible value needs confirmation
1. ✓ warns about an unusual pump rate (a likely unit slip)
1. ✓ a child: weight-based dose escalation message (high-risk calculation)
1. ✓ a weight recorded in pounds is converted before use

## Allergy class words

An allergy record that names a class ("penicillin allergy", "sulfa", "NSAIDs") is matched to these FDA Established Pharmacologic Classes (ids as published in RxClass). A word that is also an ingredient name in the singular ("tetracycline", "heparin") is matched as the ingredient; only its plural names the class. This is vocabulary, not clinical judgement; the class names below are read from the installed RxNorm subset.

| Words in the allergy record | FDA EPC classes |
|---|---|
| “penicillin”, “penicillins” | Penicillin-class Antibacterial (9 ingredients) — N0000175497 |
| “cephalosporin”, “cephalosporins” | Cephalosporin Antibacterial (22 ingredients) — N0000175488 |
| “carbapenem”, “carbapenems” | Penem Antibacterial (3 ingredients) — N0000175496 |
| “beta-lactam”, “beta-lactams”, “beta lactam”, “beta lactams” | Penicillin-class Antibacterial (9 ingredients) — N0000175497; Cephalosporin Antibacterial (22 ingredients) — N0000175488; Penem Antibacterial (3 ingredients) — N0000175496; Monobactam Antibacterial (1 ingredient) — N0000175493 |
| “sulfa”, “sulpha”, “sulfonamide”, “sulfonamides”, “sulphonamide”, “sulphonamides” | Sulfonamide Antibacterial (3 ingredients) — N0000175503; Sulfonamide Antimicrobial (2 ingredients) — N0000175504; Methylated Sulfonamide Antibacterial (1 ingredient) — N0000175511 |
| “nsaid”, “nsaids”, “non-steroidal anti-inflammatory”, “nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory” | Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drug (21 ingredients) — N0000175722 |
| “opioid”, “opioids”, “opiate”, “opiates” | Opioid Agonist (18 ingredients) — N0000175690; Opioid Agonist/Antagonist (2 ingredients) — N0000175692; Partial Opioid Agonist (1 ingredient) — N0000175689; Partial Opioid Agonist/Antagonist (1 ingredient) — N0000175688; mu-Opioid Receptor Agonist (1 ingredient) — N0000191867 |
| “macrolide”, “macrolides” | Macrolide (1 ingredient) — N0000175877; Macrolide Antibacterial (1 ingredient) — N0000175431; Macrolide Antimicrobial (3 ingredients) — N0000175935 |

## Naranjo scoring table

Source: Naranjo CA, Busto U, Sellers EM, et al. A method for estimating the probability of adverse drug reactions. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1981;30(2):239–245. Total ≥ 9 definite, 5–8 probable, 1–4 possible, ≤ 0 doubtful.

| # | Question | Yes | No | Do not know |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Are there previous conclusive reports on this reaction? | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | Did the adverse event appear after the suspected drug was administered? | 2 | -1 | 0 |
| 3 | Did the adverse reaction improve when the drug was discontinued or a specific antagonist was administered? | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 4 | Did the adverse reaction reappear when the drug was readministered? | 2 | -1 | 0 |
| 5 | Are there alternative causes (other than the drug) that could on their own have caused the reaction? | -1 | 2 | 0 |
| 6 | Did the reaction reappear when a placebo was given? | -1 | 1 | 0 |
| 7 | Was the drug detected in the blood (or other fluids) in concentrations known to be toxic? | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 8 | Was the reaction more severe when the dose was increased, or less severe when the dose was decreased? | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 9 | Did the patient have a similar reaction to the same or similar drugs in any previous exposure? | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 10 | Was the adverse event confirmed by any objective evidence? | 1 | 0 | 0 |

## WHO-UMC criteria

Source: Uppsala Monitoring Centre. The use of the WHO-UMC system for standardised case causality assessment. The category follows from the answers by fixed rules (src/rules/causality.ts, `assessUmc`), tried from the strongest category to the weakest.

- Is the information enough to judge? — Yes / Not yet — more data is needed or under examination / No — insufficient or contradictory, and it cannot be supplemented or verified
- Time relationship between drug intake and the event — Plausible / reasonable / Makes a relationship improbable (but not impossible)
- Could the disease or other drugs explain the event? — No — cannot be explained by them / unlikely to be attributed to them / Could also be explained by them / They provide a plausible explanation
- Response to withdrawal of the drug (dechallenge) — Plausible / clinically reasonable / Lacking or unclear
- Rechallenge — Positive (the event recurred) / Not done, or not needed / Negative (it did not recur)
- Is the event definitive pharmacologically or phenomenologically (an objective, specific disorder or a recognised pharmacological phenomenon)? — Yes / No
